newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq takes steps to open border with Syria.
newsitem.headline: Iraq takes steps to open border with Syria.

text.p: Iraq has taken fresh measures to open its border with Syria, closed since the beginning of the 1980s, to ease trade between the two countries, the newspaper of the ruling Baath party said on Monday.
"The Iraqi Customs Commission has taken necessary measures to open border points between Iraq and Syria," al-Thawra said, quoting head of the commission Hameed Shuker Mahmoud.
He said all necessary requirements were completed to reopen al-Qa'im border point opposite the Syrian Albukamal and al- Waleed opposite al-Tinif.
Mahmoud said the two points would handle Syrian goods that Iraq would purchase under its oil-for-food deal with the United Nations.
On Sunday, an Iraqi trade ministry source said Iraq had signed several contracts with Syrian firms to supply Baghdad with wheat, pulses, soap and detergents under the pact.
Iraqi newspapers reported on Monday that Syrian companies would soon organise in cooperation with the Health Ministry a medical exhibition in Baghdad.
They said an Iraqi economic team would discuss in a Damascus visit, which would start on June 15, trade cooperation between the two "sisterly" states.
Iraqi media have been highlighting reports of a possible rapprochement between the two Arab states, ruled by rival faction of the Arab Baath party.

Although no decision had yet been made on the resumption of both commercial and diplomatic ties, hints in this direction were first made last month during a visit of leading Syrian businessmen to Baghdad. The visit was followed by positive statements from senior officials in the two countrirs.
Syrian ties with Baghdad deteriorated in 1980 when Damascus sided with Iran in the 1980-88 Iraq-Iran war and further worsened when Syria joined the U.S.-led force that drove Iraqi troops from Kuwait.

Iraq's oil-for-food pact with the United Nations, which was extended for another 180 days on Wednesday, allows Iraq $2 billion oil exports to raise cash to buy urgent needs for Iraqis, hit by U.N. sanctions imposed for Baghdad's 1990 invasion of Kuwait.
